disposition_reason: Both ancient accounts describe the decisive defeat of the revolt but neither names the place, so it is drawn as a halo over the Watling Street corridor in the Midlands, not a pin.
title: The final defeat of Boudica's revolt
candidate_description: Suetonius Paulinus, with a much smaller force, chose a defile backed by woodland and defeated the rebel army; Boudica died soon after (by poison in Tacitus, by illness in Dio).
place: Probably along Watling Street, English Midlands (site unknown)
uncertainty_note: Neither Tacitus nor Dio names the site. It is usually placed on or near Watling Street between London and Wroxeter; candidates include Mancetter (Manduessedum) and High Cross on the Warwickshire/Leicestershire border and Church Stowe in Northamptonshire, and some writers argue for sites well outside this halo. No battlefield archaeology has been confirmed. Tacitus's figures (80,000 Britons, 400 Romans killed) are not taken as reliable. The revolt is dated AD 60 or 61: Tacitus places it (with the attack on Mona) under the consuls of 61, but many scholars read his annalistic grouping as covering 60–61 and put the outbreak in 60; the atlas uses 60 (circa) for every revolt row.
facets: Evidence type=ancient narratives|Dating basis=historical narrative|Interpretation=on or near Watling Street; Mancetter often proposed

disposition_reason: The church stands, much of it Anglo-Saxon, and is Grade I listed; its fabric includes reused Roman brick. Its building date is debated, so the row gives a window rather than a year.
title: All Saints' church, Brixworth
candidate_description: One of the largest surviving Anglo-Saxon churches in England: an aisled basilica with arcades and arches turned in reused Roman brick and tile, later given a western tower, stair turret and polygonal apse.
uncertainty_note: The building is certain; its date is not. A 12th-century Peterborough writer, Hugh Candidus, credits the foundation of a monastery at Brixworth to Cuthbald, abbot from about 675, which gave the traditional 7th-century date. Radiocarbon dates from charcoal in the construction mortar point instead to the later 8th century, and an architectural study by Fernie argued for 800–860. The window here runs from the traditional foundation to the radiocarbon date; that the monastery was Peterborough's daughter house rests on the late chronicle alone.

disposition_reason: The coin survives in the British Museum and names Offa; its copied Arabic legend dates its model to 773–774, so it was struck in Offa's reign after that. Where it was struck is unknown, so it is shown as a halo over the main Mercian-controlled mints.
title: Offa's gold dinar
candidate_description: A unique gold coin of Offa, king of Mercia (757–796), closely copying a gold dinar of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur, with the Latin words OFFA REX inserted, upside down relative to the Arabic, among the copied Arabic inscription.
place: Mercian mint, probably London or Canterbury
uncertainty_note: The coin carries no mint name and was first recorded in Rome in 1841, so where it was struck is unknown; the halo covers London and Canterbury, Offa's main mints, and is a guess. The date is a window: the model was a dinar of AH 157 (AD 773–774), and Offa died in 796. Whether it was made for trade, for a payment to Rome (Offa promised the pope 365 mancuses a year), or as a display piece is interpretation.
facets: Evidence type=gold coin (single surviving example)|Dating basis=copied Abbasid legend (AH 157, AD 773–774) and Offa's reign|Interpretation=struck for trade or for payment to Rome (debated)

disposition_reason: Three fragments of a carved and painted limestone panel were excavated under the nave of Lichfield Cathedral in 2003 and published in detail; they are dated by style to about 800, so the find is drawn at the cathedral.
title: The Lichfield Angel
candidate_description: Part of a carved panel of Ancaster limestone showing an angel, his right hand raised in blessing and a foliate sceptre in his left, still bearing traces of paint; it formed half of one end of a hollow box-like structure with a sloping lid.
uncertainty_note: The date of about 800 rests on the style of the carving, not on independent dating, so it could be some decades earlier or later. That the angel is Gabriel from an Annunciation, and that the box was a shrine chest for St Chad (d. 672), are interpretations, though widely accepted.
